chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO Accessibility for everyone. Powered by MDW Communications Affordability · Accountability · Anti-Corruption Annette Taddeo's affordability plan starts with the costs Florida families feel most: home insurance, property taxes, and power. As Florida's Chief Financial Officer, she will use the powers the office already has to grade every insurance company, mail back the money the state owes you, and audit every no-bid deal in Tallahassee.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Annette has run a small business for 30 years, creating jobs and meeting a payroll. As a mother and a business owner, she pays Florida's rising costs too. And she is not afraid to stand up to the old boys club in Tallahassee, or to anyone, in any party, to give Florida families the economic relief they deserve. Tallahassee is rigged, and you're paying for it. Florida needs a watchdog, not a lapdog. Grade every insurance company, publicly. Within her first 100 days, a report card on how fast each insurer answers claims, how often they delay or deny payment, how much of your premium goes to their own affiliates, and how financially sound they are. Naming names.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Real tax relief, with safeguards. A bigger homestead exemption, and a backstop for rural counties so a tax cut doesn't come back as a higher tax rate. Mail you the money the state owes you. Florida is holding billions in unclaimed funds. Annette's office will match the records and send you your check. Show up after the storm. Strike teams on the ground in hit communities within 3 to 5 days, helping families push stalled and lowballed claims. Post every contract. Audit every no-bid deal. Every state contract in the public FACTS database, as the law requires. No exceptions, no hiding.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Go after corruption at every level of government. Her office's sworn investigators will follow the money and refer corrupt officials for prosecution, in any party. No campaign ads on your dime. Annette will not use taxpayer money to run campaign ads. Blaise Ingoglia has spent more than $3.7 million in taxpayer money on ads right as Floridians start voting. The man who built FAFO to hunt for waste is spending your money on his own campaign. Read the fine print before you get the bill. From AI data center deals to your pension, Annette will follow the money. Every promise on this page is something the CFO's office can actually do. That's the difference between a promise and a slogan.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Affordability is the issue in this race. Here is how Annette will lower the costs Florida families can no longer keep up with. How would Annette Taddeo lower homeowners insurance costs? Annette Taddeo will publish a public report card grading every home insurance company in Florida, so you can see who pays claims and who stalls before you buy a policy. She will use her Cabinet vote to fight for lower rates and full transparency from companies that cry poor while hiding their profits. Florida homeowners pay about $8,292 a year for insurance, the highest in the nation (opens in a new tab) . For most families, the insurance bill now costs more than their property taxes.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Blaise Ingoglia, the appointed CFO who is supposed to be watching this industry, has taken at least a quarter million dollars in political contributions from insurance interests. He also voted for a $3 billion tax handout to insurance companies while they kept charging Floridians the highest rates in the nation. Publish the Insurance Company Report Card: how fast each company responds to claims, how often it delays or denies payment, how much it raises rates, how much of your premium it pays to its own affiliates, and how financially sound it is. Every company, by name.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Fight for full transparency on insurance company "affiliates," the sister companies insurers pay while claiming they are losing money here. The state's own hidden report found insurers claiming $432 million in losses while their affiliates earned $1.3 billion. (More below.) Use her Cabinet vote and the bully pulpit of the CFO's office to fight for lower rates, and demand answers when executives pay themselves millions while your premium climbs.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: The Department of Financial Services' consumer complaint records and Division of Consumer Services, the Office of Insurance Regulation's public company filings, and the CFO's seat on the Financial Services Commission, which oversees the Office of Insurance Regulation. The first report card published within her first 100 days in office, and updated every year, with every company named. What did Florida's secret insurance report find?

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Annette fought on the Senate Banking and Insurance Committee for the state to fund a study on insurance company "affiliates," only for the government to keep the report hidden for four years. It found insurers claiming losses while seeking rate increases, as their sister companies made big profits from Floridians’ premiums. Annette Taddeo will put affiliate payments on her insurance report card and use her Cabinet vote to fight for the reforms Tallahassee keeps killing.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: In 2022, the Office of Insurance Regulation paid a consultant about $150,000 to study the fees insurers pay their own affiliates, sister companies with the same owners that handle claims, underwriting, and other services. The report was never released. When the Orlando Sentinel and South Florida Sun Sentinel obtained it through a public records request, the Florida Senate demanded they destroy it (opens in a new tab) and warned of "civil or criminal legal implications."

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: The newspapers published it anyway. Across 53 companies from 2017 to 2019, insurers claimed $432 million in losses (opens in a new tab) while paying fees to affiliates that earned $1.3 billion in net income. The consultant found 20 companies paying their affiliates at rates presumed not to be "fair and reasonable," the standard in Florida law. At least 17 reported losses while paying their affiliates more than they said they lost.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: It hasn't stopped. In 2025, key Florida insurers were still paying affiliates 20 to 35 percent of premiums, the same range the report found. This year the Florida House voted 106 to 3 to give regulators more power over affiliate payments. The bill died in the Senate. State regulators now call the report flawed and outdated, but they won't say what is wrong with it. And the insurers named in it dispute its findings. Floridians paid for this report. They deserve the full picture. Blaise Ingoglia holds a vote on the Financial Services Commission, which oversees the Office of Insurance Regulation. He has said nothing.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Show you where your premium goes. Annette's insurance report card will show what share of each company's premium goes to its own affiliates, drawn from the companies' public financial filings. Use her Cabinet vote to push for an updated, independent audit of affiliate payments, the one the House promised and then dropped, and to demand the results be made public. Fight for the affiliate reform the House passed 106 to 3: a clear legal definition of "fair and reasonable" and full disclosure to regulators of what affiliates are paid. Oppose every effort to hide reports the public paid for. Your premiums, your tax dollars, your right to know.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: The CFO's seat on the Financial Services Commission, which oversees the Office of Insurance Regulation and appoints the Insurance Commissioner; the Department of Financial Services' consumer information role; and the bully pulpit. New affiliate rules need the Legislature, and Annette will fight for them. Affiliate payments listed for every company on the first insurance report card, within her first 100 days. Where does Annette Taddeo stand on property taxes and Amendment 3?

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Annette Taddeo is all in on cutting taxes for Florida homeowners, and she supports a bigger homestead exemption . But Amendment 3 has no safeguards. It could bankrupt some of Florida's rural counties, and with nothing to stop local tax rates from going back up, many families could end up paying more, not less. That's why Annette is going after the biggest bill on your house first: insurance. Amendment 3 raises the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. State economists estimate (opens in a new tab) it would take about $12 billion a year out of local budgets. The amendment does not say how any of that gets replaced.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: The hardest hit are Florida's 29 fiscally constrained rural counties, which could lose 20 to 33 percent of their yearly revenue, according to the Florida Association of Counties (opens in a new tab) . These are small counties with few businesses to share the load. Property taxes pay for their sheriffs, their firefighters, and their ambulances.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: And there is nothing in it to keep your taxes from going back up. Local governments still set their own tax rates every year, and the amendment does not limit them (opens in a new tab) . When the money has to come from somewhere, it comes from higher rates on renters, small businesses, and everything else that is still taxed. Many families could end up paying more .

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Even Republican sheriffs and Firefighters are sounding the alarm. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd (opens in a new tab) has urged voters to reject Amendment 3 and demand a plan that keeps public safety funded. The Governor now says "help for rural" (opens in a new tab) counties is coming if it passes. A promise is not a safeguard. It isn't written into the amendment. Here is the math that matters most. The average Florida homeowner pays about $8,292 a year for insurance, the highest in the nation, and far more than the typical property tax bill. If you want to put real money back in families' pockets, start with the biggest bill.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Cut taxes the right way. Annette supports raising the homestead exemption and real property tax relief, paid for honestly, with safeguards so the savings don't disappear into higher local rates and new fees. Stand with rural Florida. Annette will fight for any tax relief to come with a guaranteed backstop for fiscally constrained counties, so no community has to choose between a tax cut and a sheriff's deputy. Go after the biggest bill first. The insurance company report card (opens in a new tab) , the fight over hidden affiliate profits, and her Cabinet vote for lower rates all target the cost that is squeezing Florida homeowners hardest.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Find the money in Tallahassee first. Before anyone asks your county to cut firefighters, Annette will use the CFO's audit authority to go after the waste, no-bid contracts, and insider deals in state spending. Tell you the truth about your tax bill. If Amendment 3 passes, her office will track and publish, county by county, what happens to local budgets and tax rates, so you can see whether your tax cut was real.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Tax law is written by the Legislature and the voters, and the CFO does not set tax rates. What the CFO does have: audit authority over state spending, the state's checkbook and financial reporting, a Cabinet vote, and the bully pulpit of a statewide office. Annette will use all of them. A public, county-by-county report on local budgets and tax rates after Amendment 3, and an insurance report card in your hands within her first 100 days. Annette is for cutting your taxes. She is against a plan that defunds police and fire instead. How would Annette Taddeo fix Citizens Insurance?

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Annette Taddeo will appoint Citizens board members who answer to policyholders, not the insurance industry. The CFO directly appoints members of the Citizens Board of Governors, and Annette will use every seat she controls to put consumer champions at the table. More than 1.2 million Florida families rely on Citizens, the state-backed insurer, and every Florida policyholder is on the hook if it runs short. Families are being pushed off Citizens into private companies through "depopulation" deals. The executives of one company taking those policies collected nearly $38 million in compensation in a single year, disclosed in their own filing to Wall Street, while premiums kept climbing.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Appoint Citizens board members who answer to policyholders. Use her seat on the Financial Services Commission, which approves Citizens' plan of operation and appoints its independent Inspector General, to demand that depopulation serves families, not takeout companies. Fight for depopulation transparency: before any family is moved off Citizens, a clear, honest, side-by-side comparison of what they will pay and what coverage they will get. Direct appointment power over the Citizens Board of Governors, and the CFO's seat on the Financial Services Commission. Annette will publish the background of every Citizens board member she appoints, so you can see who they answer to.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: What will Annette Taddeo do after a hurricane? Annette Taddeo will send storm strike teams from the Department of Financial Services into hit communities within 3 to 5 days of a storm, in person, helping families push stalled and lowballed claims. No new law required. The trauma of a hurricane isn't just the premium. It's the slow-walked, lowballed claim that comes after, when families wait months for a check while living in a gutted house. Right now, when your insurer stalls, you're on your own. Deploy storm strike teams from the Division of Consumer Services into hit communities within 3 to 5 days of landfall.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Turn the state's insurance helpline into a unit with teeth: when a carrier lowballs or denies, her office will demand answers, escalate to investigators, and refer bad actors for enforcement. Expand the state's property insurance mediation program so families can fight a lowball offer without hiring a lawyer. Existing divisions of the CFO's own department: Consumer Services, the insurance fraud investigators, and the state mediation program. Given a mission and a deadline. Strike teams on the ground within 3 to 5 days of landfall, and a public report after every storm on how many claims her office helped move.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Annette Taddeo will flip the system. Instead of making you hunt for your money on a website, her office will match state records to current addresses and mail you your check. Her opponent calls your money abandoned. Annette will mail it back to you. The State of Florida is sitting on billions of dollars that belong to Florida families: dormant bank accounts, uncashed checks, forgotten insurance payouts. Roughly one in five Floridians has money waiting.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: This year, Tallahassee quietly changed the law to stop calling it your "unclaimed" money and start calling it "abandoned" property. You didn't abandon anything. The bank lost your address. A relative passed away. A check went to an old apartment. When a Florida couple went to federal court over their own $26.24 refund, the state argued they had walked away from it. The court rejected that argument. So Tallahassee changed the words in the law instead. Call your money what it is: yours. Not abandoned. Not the state's. Proactively match records to current addresses and mail you your check. Put seniors, veterans, and the families owed the most first in line for automatic returns.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: The unclaimed property program is run by the CFO's own department. No waiting on the Legislature. A public report every quarter on how much money went back into Floridians' pockets. How would Annette Taddeo help families afford a home? Annette Taddeo will fight for more down payment help and mortgage credit certificates for first-time buyers, using her Cabinet vote and audit authority over the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. She wants your kids to be able to afford to stay. Young families are being priced out of the state they grew up in, and Tallahassee has treated the housing crisis as someone else's problem.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Fight for expanded down payment assistance and mortgage credit certificates for first-time buyers. Champion homebuyer savings accounts that help working families build a down payment faster, modeled on programs already working in other states. Fight for rent payment reporting so renters who pay on time every month build the credit they deserve. Her Cabinet vote and audit authority over the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. New savings accounts and rent reporting need the Legislature, and Annette will use the bully pulpit to get them there. Annette will publish each year how much home buying help actually reached Florida families, and where. Will AI data centers raise my power bill?

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: They could, and Annette Taddeo won't wait to find out. She supports a moratorium (opens in a new tab) on new large-scale AI data centers until Florida has real, enforceable safeguards for ratepayers, water, and communities.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Massive AI data centers are coming to Florida, demanding enormous amounts of electricity and water. Tallahassee passed a law this year it said would shield ratepayers. Then Florida's biggest utility told Wall Street what the law really is: a profit engine. On its earnings call, FPL's parent company projected roughly $2 billion in guaranteed-return investment for every gigawatt of data center demand, and raised its forecast to 8 gigawatts by 2032 (opens in a new tab) . That is roughly $16 billion. The law's safeguards for you? Optional, at the discretion of a commission appointed by the Governor.

chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Energy companies have given Blaise Ingoglia over one hundred thousand dollars in political support while currently promoting the construction of massive hyperscale data centers across the state of Florida that will drive up utility costs for Florida families. Support a statewide moratorium on new large-scale AI data centers until Florida has enforceable safeguards for ratepayers, water, and communities. chunks.text: Florida drained its Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund to under $7 million during hurricane and brush fire season, after roughly $890 million in spending. chunks.text: Florida Statutes require it (opens in a new tab) . Once a state of emergency lasts more than a year, all of its spending must be audited, and updated every year. chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Blaise Ingoglia built an audit operation, which he named FAFO, to go after county governments across the state. chunks.text: Track every dollar of federal reimbursement Florida is eligible for and report on what has actually come back. Florida is eligible for up to $608 million from FEMA. chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Yes. Annette Taddeo will apply one standard to every level of government, in any party. chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Start where the money is: the state contracts and emergency spending Blaise Ingoglia refuses to examine. Publish audit findings in plain language so every Floridian can follow the money. chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO
chunks.text: Enforce the law. Every contract goes in the FACTS database. No exceptions, no hiding contracts as purchase orders. chunks.title: The Issues — Annette Taddeo for Florida CFO

chunks.title: Meet Annette Taddeo — Annette Taddeo for Chief Financial Officer
chunks.text: When Annette Taddeo’s father — an American fighter pilot who served in World War II and Korea — was kidnapped by FARC guerrillas in Colombia, her family fled to the United States with everything that mattered: resilience, a commitment to public service, and the belief that hard work still meant something in America. She built LanguageSpeak from the ground up into one of America’s top 500 small businesses, raised a family in Miami-Dade, and won a State Senate seat — and then kept winning it. In Tallahassee, she earned respect across party lines by doing one thing consistently: standing up for Florida families, no matter who was in her way.

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture Farmers are Florida’s first environmentalists. When you pull your living out of the ground everyday, you know just how sacred that is and how much the conservation of our natural resources matters. Making Meaningful Progress in the Everglades Rural and Family Lands Protection Program As a member of the Florida Cabinet, Wilton stood with Governor Ron DeSantis in May 2023 to approve the preservation of approximately 18,279.38 acres of working agricultural land through cost-effective conservation easements totaling nearly $58 million.

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: The preservation efforts will prevent future development of the land and allow agriculture operations to continue to contribute to Florida’s economy and the production of food, timber, and other resources vital to the prosperity of the Sunshine State. These nine acquisitions are the largest through the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services’ Rural and Family Lands Protection Program ever approved in the history of the program. “Food security is a matter of national security, and by protecting and preserving lands that have an immense amount of economic impact to food and agricultural production in our state, we are securing the livelihood of Florida.”

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Wilton Has Delivered Key Investments in Florida’s Environment A lot of folks talk about the need for critical investments in Florida’s environment, but Wilton has actually done the work. Prioritizing water and land conservation, Wilton has fought for billions of dollars to ensure our precious environment is preserved for future generations of Floridians. From the Everglades Restoration Act to the Florida Wildlife Corridor Act and his steadfast commitment to restoring our springs, Wilton has been a champion for Florida’s environment. Just this year, Wilton sent a budget to Governor Ron DeSantis that included more than a billion dollars in key investments in our environment.

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: $64 million to continue fully funding the Everglades Agricultural Area (EAA) Reservoir $288 million to support the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan More than $73 million for the Northern Everglades Estuaries Program $450 million for Aquifer Storage and Recovery (ASR) $782 million for water quality improvements to further support ongoing efforts to address water concerns across the state. This includes investments in Piney Point Cleanup ($100 million), Rattlesnake Key ($23 million) and Biscayne Bay ($20 million).

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: $26 million investment in the effort to stem red tide through research and for red tide mitigation. This builds on the $70 million in red tide funding and an additional $68 million for blue-green algae funding invested over the previous four years. $10.8 million investment for the implementation of the Blue-Green Algae Task Force recommendations. The Blue-Green Algae Task Force will prioritize projects to expedite nutrient reduction in Lake Okeechobee and the St. Lucie and Caloosahatchee estuaries.

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: The Rural and Family Lands Program is critical for preserving Florida’s natural resources while allowing agricultural operations to continue to fuel our food supply chain. chunks.text: “As a result of your ongoing support and our community’s relentless dedication to this work, our ecosystem is once again teaming with fish, manatees, crabs, birds, and a clean, healthy environment for both local citizens and the millions of visitors that come to our country from all over the world each year.” — Lisa Moore, President, Save Crystal River Established a Statewide Infrastructure Plan

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: This plan prioritizes investing in state and local affordable housing programs, mitigates the impacts of sea level rise and enhances wastewater programs, including septic-to-sewer conversions. He worked to foundationally change the way our state uses tax revenue from documentary stamps, which people have to pay when they buy property. The new framework provides predictable funding for all three infrastructure priorities each and every year. Floridians have been waiting a long time for comprehensive policy and budget planning that addresses these three critical areas of public policy and this plan makes it a reality.

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: “It is crucial that we modernize our documentary stamp distributions to dedicate a steady stream of funding in three key areas of infrastructure – affordable housing, wastewater, and mitigation of sea-level rise.” — Wilton Simpson Preserved & Protected Important Green Infrastructure

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Under Wilton’s leadership, the Legislature prioritized funding to create incentives for conservation and sustainable development while conserving the green infrastructure that is the foundation of Florida’s economy and quality of life.  The Florida Wildlife Corridor Act ensures the Florida maintains critical wildlife habitats and that we protect the headwaters of major watersheds, including the Everglades and the St. Johns River.

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: These efforts are critical as we work to address flooding and sea-level rise resiliency as well as water management and prescribed burns essential for land management and restoration. Preserving and protecting these land and water resources is not only vital to wildlife but critical to our groundwater recharge that provides drinking water to Florida communities. Additionally, this legislation will help sustain Florida’s working ranches, farms, and forests that are home to many wildlife habitats. “Florida made conservation history by enacting a bill and securing $400 million in funding to help protect the state’s vast network of natural areas.”

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Expedited the Implementation of the Lake Okeechobee Watershed Restoration Under Wilton’s leadership as Senate President, Florida law now calls for expedited implementation of the Lake Okeechobee Watershed Restoration Project. This project is the most important element of restoration for the northern Everglades ecosystem, as approximately 95 percent of the water, 92 percent of the phosphorus, and 89 percent of the nitrogen flowing into Lake Okeechobee comes from north of the lake.

chunks.title: Environment | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Northern storage can be used to help keep lake levels from rising too high in the wet season and make water available for release in the dry season. This creates the flexibility necessary to help better maintain lake levels and ensure adequate water supply for users around the lake when water is needed during dry periods. “If you want to understand how our environment works in theory, ask a scientist. chunks.title: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture Wilton understands firsthand that the security of a safe and loving family are foundational to who we are and has fought to protect the unborn, our most vulnerable children and our seniors. Wilton is 100% pro-life and believes we have a moral obligation to protect the unborn. Wilton believes that every abortion kills a special and unique human being who deserves protection under the laws of this state and the chance to grow up in a loving family. With the United States Supreme Court set to hear a similar law, in 2022, Wilton fought to prohibit abortion after 15 weeks.

chunks.title: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: In 2020, Wilton worked to secure parental consent for termination of a pregnancy and to protect infants born alive. As a result, Florida law requires that a physician must obtain written consent from a parent or legal guardian before performing an abortion on a minor. Growing up as an adopted child in a family that took in foster children, it has always been important to Wilton that our state do everything we can to promote adoption as an alternative to abortion. Floridians can be proud that we live in a state that not only protects innocent, unborn life, but also supports children and parents. Wilton has led the charge to create consistency for Florida’s most vulnerable children.

chunks.title: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Adopted as a child, reforming Florida’s child welfare system isn’t just a talking point for Wilton, it’s personal. Wilton prioritized the safety and stability of children in the state system with the goal of improving both present living conditions and future outcomes for the children entrusted to our welfare system. The comprehensive reforms range from training to reporting, placement changes, transparency and accountability. Wilton also worked to ensure a number of resources to former foster care youth participating in the Road-to-Independence Program.

chunks.title: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Wilton’s focus has expanded and clarified Florida’s laws related to sibling and transition placements for children in out-of-home care; and recognizes and balances relationships young children develop with out-of-home caregivers and siblings with those of the child’s biological family members, in order to reduce trauma related to abrupt or frequent placement changes that remove children from safe, successful placements.

chunks.title: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Wilton has fought to ensure parents are the primary decision makers for their children, not government. The Parents’ Bill of Rights prevents the state and public schools from infringing on the fundamental rights of parents to direct the upbringing of their child when it comes to education, health care and mental health.

chunks.title: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: Thanks to the Parents’ Bill of Rights, only a parent can make religious upbringing or health decisions for a child. A parent must grant permission for their child to get any type of biometric scan, blood type records or for DNA to be collected, limits when video can be taken of a child and requires consent from a parent before law enforcement can access education records in most cases. Wilton also fought to allow public school students to use Hope Scholarships to transfer to a private school or to another public school if they feel they face “harassment” in response to their COVID-related decisions. That includes decisions against wearing a mask.

chunks.title: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture
chunks.text: “The pandemic has shown that parents sometimes need alternatives to their assigned school. Wilton Simpson responded by expanding programs that empower families to customize their children’s education experience.” — John Kirtley Co-Chair, Florida Federation for Children

chunks.title: Families | Wilton Simpson, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida This Isn't About Party. It's About People. The challenges facing Florida families aren't left or right. They're real. And they demand real solutions. Politics has spent years dividing people over labels while the actual problems kept getting worse. Housing costs that make it impossible to stay. Schools that are underfunded and over-politicized. A health care system that's too expensive to rely on for too many families. Climate impacts that threaten coastal communities and drive up insurance rates. These aren't talking points. They're the lived experience of working families across Florida.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: The question isn't where a solution comes from. The question is whether it makes life better. Solving our Affordability and Insurance Crisis

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: The property insurance crisis is the primary reason so many people in Florida are struggling to afford a place to live. From renters to retirees to homeowners, the burden of property insurance continues to make housing costs in Florida unaffordable for many. A state catastrophic fund that removes natural disaster risk from the private insurance market would dramatically reduce property and car insurance rates, restoring affordability and price stability for millions of Floridians. Allowing condominium associations and owners access to a no-interest state-backed loan program would likewise address the crushing financial burden of generational condominium repairs.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Delivering Affordable Healthcare to Floridians Medicaid is a critical program for Florida. It supports childbirth care for women and infants, long-term care for seniors, care for those with special needs and unique abilities, and is a critical funding source for hospitals across the state. In the face of cuts from Washington and Tallahassee, Florida should commit to expanding Medicaid and ensuring healthcare for all Floridians.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Public schools have been inadequately funded in the state of Florida for decades. We need to dramatically increase investment in Florida's public schools to provide higher quality public schools in more neighborhoods, with more teachers who earn a more competitive salary. Schools in Florida's private school voucher program need to meet the same high standards as our public schools. Private schools that accept vouchers should be required to provide the same specialized services public schools provide and not charge additional tuition. The voucher program should be means-tested to ensure funding is provided for families with demonstrated economic need.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Hyperscale data centers strain Florida's water, power, and an already strained aquifer, destabilize the neighborhoods around them, and have yet to prove a long-term economic payoff beyond the construction jobs. Floridians from Palm Beach County to Lakeland have already said no. Florida needs an immediate moratorium on the construction of hyperscale data centers, issued on day one, until the environmental impact is fully studied, the protections for water and communities are proven sufficient, and the people who live here have a real say in what gets built next door.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Florida has some of the weakest ethics and campaign finance rules of any state in the country. Incumbent politicians solicit unlimited money from corporations in clear relationship to official acts. Florida should lead the nation in campaign finance reform and a sweeping ethics package committed to transparency and to protecting Florida taxpayers from legalized graft in Tallahassee.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Florida has one of the largest economies in the world, but it has been hindered by short-term political thinking. Florida should become a leading technology economy and invest in a renewed agriculture economy with a vision for the next century. We should continue to grow our tourist economy and should retain Florida's top talent while attracting the world's brightest minds and creators.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Reproductive healthcare decisions should be made between women and their doctors, not politicians. Roe v. Wade and Casey v. Planned Parenthood provided a responsible, balanced framework for protecting these decisions. Absent federal legislation restoring these protections, Florida should codify the Roe/Casey framework. Investing in Climate Resiliency, Clean Water, and the Ocean Economy

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Florida is home to remarkable ecosystems, waterways, and coastlines. The state's management of these resources has been insufficient. Florida should accept the science of climate change, protect our beaches and state parks, and invest in resiliency throughout the state. Florida should adopt a sustainability agenda that conserves our natural resources and grows an economy reliant on tourism, fisheries, hospitality, and outdoor living.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Florida is home to one of the largest veteran populations in the United States. We are fortunate to have men and women from all generations who have honorably served across all service branches. In the face of federal cuts and drawback of services, Florida should lead the nation in filling the gap of critical services for those who have served our nation in uniform. Giving Florida's Families Access to Florida's Universities

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Too many Florida families are locked out of our state's flagship universities. Florida is fortunate to be home to some of our nation's leading colleges and universities, but it only benefits Florida families if our students can gain admission. Qualified Florida students should have preferred application status for Florida's universities.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Florida suffers needlessly from gun violence. Responsible gun owners are not the problem, but lax gun laws are. Its time politicians in Tallahassee do more, protecting responsible gun owners' rights while passing common-sense reforms. Florida should ban the sale of assault weapons, require universal and comprehensive background checks, explore licensing, and preserve and expand the red flag laws enacted following the tragedy at Parkland.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Florida leaders should unleash clean and renewable energies across the Sunshine State, requiring greater integration of clean energy technologies into our public utilities. Environmentally sound energy technologies provide for greater stewardship of our environment, protect our tourist and environmental economy, and can drive down utility costs for all Florida consumers.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Across Florida, voters continue to use their vote to choose the direction of their state and their community. But Tallahassee politicians preempt the will of the voters based on selfish ideological whims. Direct democracy in Florida should be easier, not harder. Florida should respect home rule, and support the implementation of successful voter initiatives in communities across the state. Florida should make constitutional amendments easier for voters to place on the ballot, and if an amendment gets more than 50% of the vote, the Governor should fight to enact it on behalf of the people.

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Whether you're a native born Floridian, an immigrant to our state, or a Tallahassee politician, if you break the law in Florida, you'll be held accountable. But Florida can also be a state that corrects disparities in criminal justice for communities of color and immigrant communities, promoting local control of community policing. It's time Florida fights crime, not communities. Treating Everyone with Kindness, Dignity and Respect

chunks.title: Issues: David Jolly’s Policy Positions for Florida
chunks.text: Culture wars divide and demonize. Florida should reject the politics of division and hate, and instead create a home where everyone is valued, respected, and welcomed. We should become a place where everyone is given dignity and treated equally, regardless of race, creed, or color; and regardless of who you love or who you worship. Florida should embrace our immigrant community and celebrate their contributions to our state's culture and economy. It's time to create a Florida for all people. Not better talking points. Not better excuses. Better outcomes for the people who live here. That's what this campaign is about. That's what leadership should deliver.

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor David Jolly's Plan to Cut Florida Homeowners Insurance by 60 to 70 Percent Floridians pay the highest home insurance prices in America because every family is made to pay a private insurer to carry hurricane risk. Jolly's proposal moves that risk into one strong, state-backed fund. Here is how it works, what it costs, and what it saves.

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: David Jolly's plan creates a state-backed hurricane fund to carry hurricane and wind risk, which makes up 60 to 70 percent of Florida homeowners insurance bills. Private insurers would no longer price hurricane risk into policies, cutting costs by an estimated 64 percent (about $4,500 a year for a $300,000 home, dropping from $7,136 to $2,557). The fund is paid for by making insurance companies pay taxes they currently avoid and other sources that do not burden homeowners, with coverage starting only after the fund is financially sound and backed by reinsurance. What hurricane risk costs a Florida family today

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: Insure.com's Florida home insurance calculator, for a $300,000 home with a $1,000 deductible: the average policy priced with hurricane risk, and the same policy priced without it. Floridians are paying the highest home insurance prices in America, and the private market has collapsed. Company after company has pulled out of the state or gone under, and the ones that remain price every policy for the worst storm they can imagine, because in Florida the worst storm is not hypothetical.

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: The main reason a Florida policy costs so much more than one in Georgia or Ohio is one line on the bill: hurricane and wind. That single risk can be 60 to 70 percent of what a family pays. Every other part of a homeowners policy—fire, theft, liability, a burst pipe—is priced roughly the way it is priced anywhere else. Instead of forcing every Florida family to pay a private insurer to take on that enormous hurricane risk, Jolly's proposal does four things, in order. Florida creates one strong, state-backed hurricane fund. One fund, for the whole state, carrying hurricane and wind risk for Florida homes.

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: The fund is built to a financially sound level and buys backup insurance for catastrophic storms. Coverage does not start until enough money is set aside and reinsurance for the biggest storms is in place. The fund is built first; it does not borrow against a storm that has not happened. The fund is paid for without putting the burden back on homeowners. Insurance companies would start paying the taxes they currently avoid. Other sources that do not put a burden on homeowners, such as a fee on real estate transactions or existing tourist taxes, are on the table. The Legislature writes the specific funding policy. How the fund is paid for, in detail.

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: Private insurers no longer have to price hurricane risk into your policy. That is where the 60 to 70 percent savings comes from. The rest of your policy stays private, competitive, and priced the way policies are in other states. Florida already has a state catastrophic fund. The Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund was created in a special legislative session in November 1993, after Hurricane Andrew, and it has been run and expanded by Republican legislatures for three decades. Right now, that fund only reimburses insurance companies for a share of their hurricane losses. It is a bailout for insurers.

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: David Jolly's plan takes a structure Florida has already proven and directs it to the people who actually pay the bills. Does Florida already have a hurricane catastrophe fund? The fund is rolled out responsibly. Coverage becomes available only after a fiscally sound amount of money is set aside and backup reinsurance is in place. The Legislature is involved in creating the specific policies, including the funding. And in the end, the costs will be lower for Floridians, or we won't do it. Simple as that.

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: Byron Donalds is running ads claiming this proposal creates a "$1,000 hurricane tax." It does not. The ad's two "sources" are a legislative feasibility study that did not look at Jolly's proposal and an opinion blog post. When reporters asked Donalds about the number, he didn't give them a source; instead, he referred to an entirely different, unrelated law. We answer the claim, and the study, on their own pages: Does David Jolly want a $1,000 hurricane tax? What is the study Byron Donalds cites in his hurricane tax ad? Will David Jolly's catastrophe fund raise costs for Floridians? What is Byron Donalds' plan to lower insurance costs?

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: "Losing campaigns lie. What Byron is doing is using fear to try to stop progress." David Jolly, September 14, 2026. Q. How much would David Jolly's plan save on homeowners insurance? Hurricane and wind risk can be 60 to 70 percent of a Florida homeowners bill. Based on Insure.com's Florida home insurance calculator, a $300,000 home with a $1,000 deductible averages $7,136 a year when the policy is priced with hurricane risk and $2,557 when it is not. That is a 64 percent difference, about $4,500 a year. Q. Who pays for the state catastrophe fund?

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: Not homeowners. The plan funds it by making insurance companies pay the taxes they currently avoid, and through other sources that do not put the burden back on homeowners, such as a fee on real estate transactions or existing tourist taxes. The Legislature writes the specific funding policy. Only after the fund reaches a fiscally sound level and backup reinsurance for catastrophic storms is in place. The fund is built first, then it covers people. Q. Does Florida already have something like this?

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: Yes. The Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund has existed since 1993. Today it reimburses insurance companies for a share of their hurricane losses; it does not cover homeowners directly. The plan applies a structure Florida has already proven to the people who pay the bills. Q. Is there a $1,000 hurricane tax in the plan? No. There is no $1,000 fee, tax or assessment on homeowners in the plan. The claim comes from a Byron Donalds ad whose sources are a legislative feasibility study of a different proposal and an opinion blog post. The full answer is at /homeowners-insurance/hurricane-tax/.

chunks.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance Plan: David Jolly for Governor
chunks.text: The plan and its numbers are from the Jolly campaign's published proposal and its September 2026 statement on the Donalds ads. The premium comparison is from Insure.com's Florida homeowners insurance calculator for a $300,000 dwelling with a $1,000 deductible, comparing the policy priced with a hurricane deductible against the standard policy. The history of the Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund is from the State Board of Administration , which runs it. David Jolly's remarks are from his September 14, 2026 video press conference and from Florida Phoenix . This page was last reviewed on September 15, 2026 and is re-verified as the story develops.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly Florida Should Be a Place You Can Afford to Call Home From the rent check to the insurance bill, the cost of living here has outrun the paychecks of the people who make Florida run.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Our plan takes on Florida's affordability crisis in several ways. Let's start with housing and insurance.It dramatically lowers insurance premiums by creating a statewide catastrophic fund. It reduces monthly electric bills by capping utility company profits. It scales up workforce and affordable housing construction with down-payment assistance for first-time buyers. Our plan protects renters through expanded affordable housing programs and, to help condo owners cover special assessments, it offers no-interest state-backed loans. It's an actual plan, not an empty promise, to leave Florida families with more money at the end of each month.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: For generations, Florida meant a fresh start, a house with a yard, and the room to build a life. Now young families are watching that promise fade as the typical first-time buyer waits until age 40, and even lifelong Floridians open their insurance bills with dread. This is not just an economic problem. It is about whether working people can still put down roots in the state they love.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: No family should have to choose between insuring their home and keeping the lights on. Florida pays the highest homeowners' premiums in the country, and too many carriers have walked away, leaving people stranded. We will fight for a system that treats hurricane risk as the shared statewide challenge it is, so a single storm season doesn't decide whether you keep your house. Read the full plan: how a state-backed catastrophe fund cuts Florida homeowners insurance by 60 to 70 percent.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Electricity is not a luxury, and over-the-top profits for the biggest utilities should not come out of your monthly budget. Florida regulators have let investor-owned power companies earn some of the fattest returns in the nation while families ration the air conditioning in the summer heat. We will push to cap utility profits in line with the national average and put that money back where it belongs, in your pocket.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: You cannot fix a shortage by wishing it away, and Florida is short the homes its growing families need. We will invest in the tools that work, from workforce housing to real down-payment help for first-time buyers, so a nurse, a teacher, or a young couple can find a place they can afford. Building more is how we bring prices back within reach. Protect Renters and Condo Owners Left Behind

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Half of Florida renters now hand over more than a third of their income just to keep a roof overhead, and older condo owners are being hit with special assessments that can wipe out a lifetime of savings. Safety matters, and no one should live in an unsafe building, but families cannot be left to shoulder impossible bills alone. We will stand with renters and long-time owners so the fine print doesn't force them out of their own homes.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: When most people can't cover a surprise bill without going into debt, the whole economy is one storm away from crisis. Real affordability means an honest shot at saving, not just surviving the next deductible or rate hike. Every fight on this page comes back to one goal: leaving Florida families with more at the end of the month. Florida can be a place where hard work still buys a home, a full fridge, and a night's sleep without worry. Let's build that Florida together. Q. Why can't I afford to buy a home in Florida anymore?

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Florida's median home price reached $420,000, mortgage rates sit around 6.36 percent, and insurance premiums are among the nation's highest. Long-term owners pay far less property tax than new buyers for the same house thanks to Save Our Homes caps, and the structural result is that the median first-time buyer age has risen sharply. Q. How will this plan help me if I rent? More than half of Florida renters now pay over 30 percent of income on housing. The plan scales workforce and affordable housing targeted near job centers, expands existing state housing programs, and caps utility profits to lower the monthly bills renters pay on top of rent.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. What if I own an older condo and got hit with a huge special assessment? Older coastal condos have been hit hardest by new inspection requirements, with many owners facing assessments of $50,000 or more per unit. The plan offers no-interest state-backed loans so associations can spread costs over time without forcing fixed-income owners to sell. Q. What if I am a hospitality worker in Tampa or Orlando? The plan specifically calls for scaling workforce housing based on income and proximity to work, deliberately targeting tourism corridors rather than scattered housing. The utility profit cap would also lower monthly bills, and the proximity to work framing should reduce commute costs.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. What are average home insurance premiums in Florida right now? Estimates range from roughly $5,400 to $15,000 per year depending on home value and coverage level. Every credible analysis ranks Florida at or near the top nationally, with coastal markets like Miami-Dade, Tampa, and Jacksonville seeing the largest increases. Q. Won't capping utility profit hurt investment in Florida's grid? The cap would bring Florida's authorized utility return in line with the national average of roughly 9 to 10 percent. Utilities in other states earning that rate continue to invest in grid modernization and storm hardening, there is no evidence that matching the national norm suppresses investment.

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. Will a state catastrophic insurance fund just be a taxpayer bailout for risky homes? No, it is a risk-pooling mechanism that lowers costs for everyone by spreading hurricane exposure across all Florida homes. Homeowners still pay for their state hurricane coverage, just at a lower combined cost than today's system where each private insurer prices in huge risk margins. Q. What about retirees on fixed income in Florida?

chunks.title: Affordable Housing in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Retirees face acute pressures from condo special assessments and rising property insurance. The no-interest state-backed condo loan is targeted directly at fixed-income condo owners who can't absorb a six-figure special assessment, and the catastrophic fund insurance savings would also hit hardest for retirees who often pay insurance directly. In depth The Florida I Remember (And What We're Losing) In depth As Governor - Affordability Housing

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly No one should be one diagnosis away from fear, delay, or debt. David Jolly's health care plan for Florida expands Medicaid to cover hundreds of thousands of uninsured Floridians and invests in more primary care clinics throughout the state so people can access care when and where they need it, regardless of income. Medicaid expansion can start within months once the Legislature approves it, with coverage beginning in the first year. Jolly proposes a five-year pilot to dramatically expand community health centers in every Florida county so care is available, not just coverage on paper. A Plan as Governor to Improve Health Care

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: This system isn't working for the people who need it. Across Florida, families are making impossible choices when it comes to health care. Going without insurance. Delaying treatment. Hoping that what they are dealing with doesn't get worse. Not because they don't care about their health. But because the system makes it too expensive, too complicated, and too uncertain. No one should have to wonder whether they can afford to get care. No one should be forced to choose between their health and their financial stability. And yet, that's exactly where too many people find themselves.

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Expanding Medicaid is part of the solution. It would provide coverage to hundreds of thousands of Floridians who are currently left without access to care. Because access isn't just about coverage. It's about whether care is actually available when and where people need it. That's why Florida should invest in more primary healthcare clinics throughout the state. Places where people can go, regardless of income, to receive basic care, support, and treatment. Not as a long-term substitute for a better system. But as a way to make sure people aren't left waiting while bigger solutions take shape. Health care should be built around people. Not barriers.

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: And right now, there are too many barriers standing in the way. Getting care shouldn't feel like a risk. It should feel within reach for every Floridian. Join the fight for accessible health care in Florida Real solutions start with real action. Stand with David Jolly to expand health care access across Florida. Q. Why isn't Medicaid expansion enough on its own? Because expansion provides coverage, but people still need somewhere to actually get care. Jolly proposes a 5-year pilot to dramatically expand community health centers in every Florida county so new enrollees can connect with primary care providers, not just have coverage on paper.

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. How long would this plan take to actually help me? Medicaid expansion can start within months once the Legislature approves it, with coverage beginning in the first year. Scaling community health centers takes longer, which is why Jolly proposes a 5-year build to create durable access alongside the immediate coverage. Q. Does this plan raise my taxes as a Florida resident? No. The plan uses Florida tax dollars already being collected, paired with a 9-to-1 federal match. The state share is offset by reduced emergency care costs, lower uncompensated care payments, and increased tax revenue from a stronger healthcare workforce. Q. How would this plan affect rural Floridians?

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Rural counties have been hit hardest by healthcare gaps. Jolly's plan scales community health centers in every county, including rural areas where private practices are unviable, and stabilizes rural hospital revenue by reducing uncompensated care through Medicaid expansion. Q. What if I am a small business owner in Florida? Small businesses struggle to offer coverage because they cannot get the group rates large employers negotiate. Medicaid expansion would let your lowest-paid workers have a coverage option instead of being stuck in the coverage gap, and it stabilizes the market where you and your employees buy insurance. Q. How does Florida rank for healthcare nationally?

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Poorly across most measures. Florida has one of the highest uninsured rates in the country at 15.5% for working-age adults, ranks among the worst states for maternal mortality, and has about 266,000 adults shut out of both Medicaid and marketplace subsidies. Q. What if the federal government cuts the 90% match?

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: The 90% match is set in statute, not annual appropriation, which means it cannot be changed without an act of Congress. Any change would also disrupt 41 states' Medicaid programs, including red states like Indiana and Ohio, which makes a partisan cut politically difficult. Florida could adopt trigger provisions that would automatically roll back expansion if the federal match drops below a certain level. Q. How would this plan affect Florida hospitals?

chunks.title: Health Care Reform in Florida – David Jolly
chunks.text: Florida hospitals would see two direct benefits. First, Medicaid expansion would shift much of the uncompensated care burden to the federal government at the 90% match rate. Second, scaling community health centers reduces preventable ER visits by triaging patients in primary care. In depth Why Florida's Next Governor Will Fire the Surgeon General

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida Public education shouldn't be an afterthought. Florida families deserve real opportunity. And that starts with strong public schools. David Jolly believes public education should be Florida's foundation, not an afterthought. His plan focuses on paying teachers what they deserve, investing in school infrastructure and resources, and ensuring every child has access to strong public schools regardless of zip code. He argues Florida needs a public education renaissance, not abandonment, because strong public schools strengthen communities, support families, and build the workforce Florida's future depends on.

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: This isn't what real school choice looks like. For years, Florida politicians have talked about school choice as if it is the answer to everything. But for many families, that “choice” doesn’t actually exist. Because when public schools are underfunded, understaffed, and left behind, families aren’t choosing between great options. And too often, that system has shifted education into the hands of for-profit institutions, while the public schools that serve the majority of Florida’s children are asked to do more with less. That’s not a real solution. It’s a system that leaves too many students behind.

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Public education should be the foundation. The place where every child, regardless of zip code, has access to opportunity, support, and a real path forward. But that only happens when we invest in it. That means paying teachers what they deserve. Supporting the people who show up every day to educate, guide, and inspire the next generation. It means investing in school infrastructure, classrooms, and resources so students aren’t trying to learn in systems that have been neglected for too long. And it means recognizing that strong public schools don’t just benefit students. They strengthen communities, support families, and build the workforce that Florida’s future depends on.

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Florida doesn’t need to abandon public education. That starts with schools we are willing to invest in. Get involved in the fight for Florida's public schools Q. Why are so many teachers leaving Florida? Florida opened the 2024-25 school year with nearly 10,000 vacant positions, including over 5,000 teacher roles. The main reason is pay: Florida's average teacher salary ranks 50th of 51 states nationally (only Mississippi is worse), and teachers also cite high cost of living and Florida's political climate as reasons to leave. Q. What does Jolly want to do about teacher pay?

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Jolly wants to dramatically increase teacher pay as part of a 10-year public education renaissance. He proposes redirecting Tourist Development Tax revenue (currently used for convention centers and tourism promotion) toward teacher pay and school infrastructure, which would require legislative change. Q. How does Jolly plan to fund his education priorities? Jolly proposes expanding the allowed uses of Florida's Tourist Development Tax (over $1 billion per year statewide) to include teacher pay and school infrastructure. His framing: Florida doesn't have a crisis of convention centers, it has a crisis of public education. Q. What about rural Florida school districts?

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Rural districts face compounding challenges: shrinking enrollment, higher per-pupil costs, and the most severe teacher shortages (especially in special education, science, and math). Jolly's plan to raise teacher pay statewide would help rural districts compete for talent, and expanded state funding would help them maintain operations as local tax bases decline. Q. How are Florida public schools currently funded? Florida K-12 public schools are funded primarily through the Florida Education Finance Program (FEFP), which combines state appropriations, local property tax revenue, and federal funds. Florida's per-pupil spending is approximately $12,400, ranking 8th lowest among U.S. states.

chunks.title: David Jolly on Public Education in Florida
chunks.text: Q. Is the federal government taking over education policy? No. Federal funding is under 10% of total K-12 spending, and federal law explicitly gives states control over curriculum, funding, teacher policy, and school choice. State-level governance (governor and legislature) is the dominant driver of school quality, which is why a Florida governor's education plan has more impact on Florida students than any federal change.

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly David Jolly believes protecting Florida's environment is essential to the state's economy and quality of life. His plan calls for real investments in environmental protection, accelerated clean and renewable energy integration into Florida's utility system, sustained funding for coastal resiliency and water quality improvements, and honest climate planning in state policy. David sees environmental protection as protecting what makes Florida successful: the tourism economy, clean beaches, healthy waters, and the natural beauty that families depend on every day. This is about more than the environment.

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: For families across Florida, the environment isn't an abstract issue. It's part of everyday life. It's the beaches they visit and parks they play in. The water they drink and air they breathe. The places that make this state feel like home. For David and his family, it's deeply personal. Time spent near the ocean, watching their kids experience the same natural beauty that defines so much of Florida. That connection is something millions of Floridians share. And yet, too often, protecting it is treated like a secondary concern. Something to debate. Something to delay. But the truth is, Florida's environment isn't separate from its success.

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Our economy depends on it. Tourism. Fishing. Local businesses. Entire communities rely on clean water, healthy coastlines, and a natural environment that people want to experience and protect. When that is threatened, it's not just an environmental issue. It's an economic one. It's a quality of life issue. It's a future issue. Protecting Florida's environment means making real investments. Taking real responsibility. And refusing to treat long-term damage as acceptable. It means understanding that what we protect today is what we pass on tomorrow. Because once it's gone, it's not coming back. Florida's future depends on what we protect today. Q. Is my insurance crisis related to climate?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Yes, structurally. Florida's property insurance crisis is driven by hurricane risk, litigation costs, and reinsurance prices, and the hurricane risk component has grown with warming ocean temperatures and rising sea levels. Insurers price policies to absorb rising expected losses, so climate is one of the underlying drivers of the insurance crisis. Yes, and Florida faces some of the most direct climate impacts in the country. Florida's Gulf Coast is projected for 22 to 26 inches of sea level rise by 2050 (about double the U.S. average), and hurricane intensity is rising. The 2024 hurricane season caused over $100 billion in combined damage across the Southeast.

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Q. What does David Jolly want to do about clean energy? Jolly's position is to unleash clean and renewable energies across Florida, requiring greater integration of clean energy technologies into public utilities. This means stronger net metering rules to support rooftop solar and accelerated utility-scale renewable buildout. Florida is projected to receive $62.7 billion in IRA-funded clean power investment by 2030. Q. Aren't climate policies just going to hurt the Florida economy?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: The economic case runs the other way. Florida's tourism economy ($134 billion in visitor spending, 1.8 million jobs), ocean economy, and saltwater fishing industry ($9.2 billion in annual impact) all depend on a healthy environment. Climate policy in Florida protects the state's largest industries rather than imposing costs against them. Q. What about Floridians who live in coastal communities?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Coastal Floridians face the most direct climate exposure: rising sea levels, more intense hurricanes, and accelerating beach erosion. David Jolly's plan calls for wiser coastal development practices and sustained investment in resiliency, which means living shorelines and hybrid systems, seawalls where necessary and appropriate, raised infrastructure, beach renourishment where cost-effective and sustainable, stormwater drainage upgrades, and building code modernization in coastal counties. Q. How would David Jolly handle Florida's water quality crises?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Jolly's plan ties water quality to broader environmental investment. Blue-green algae crises are addressed by reducing discharges of nutrient pollution to our coastal waters, and springs degradation is addressed through septic to sewer conversions, agricultural runoff rules, and groundwater protection. Protecting Florida's coast requires changing what flows into it. Q. What about FPL and renewable energy under David Jolly?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Jolly's clean energy position would require greater integration of renewables into Florida's utility planning. That likely means stronger net metering rules to support rooftop solar and accelerated utility-scale renewable buildout, pushing FPL and other utilities to expand renewable generation. Q. Why oppose offshore drilling if it could create Florida jobs?

chunks.title: Protecting Florida’s Environment & Climate – David Jolly
chunks.text: Offshore drilling creates very few Florida jobs because rigs are based out of Louisiana and Texas ports. What Florida loses in a spill (tourism revenue, fishing industry, real estate value, ecological damage) runs to tens of billions of dollars. Florida's tourism economy ($130 billion) and ocean economy ($30 billion) depend on clean beaches and healthy water.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026 Before the labels. Before the noise. There's the person and the choices that shaped him. David Jolly is a former Member of Congress, attorney, and fifth-generation Floridian running for Florida Governor in 2026. His campaign focuses on historic homeowner's insurance reform, expanding primary healthcare services, and investing in community public schools. Jolly believes everyone deserves access to work, wages, and wealth, with rights protected and dignity celebrated regardless of background. People will try to tell you who David Jolly is. This page lets you hear it for yourself. Not through labels. Not through talking points.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: Chapter One: Not a politician. A person. Before anything else, this starts with the person. Faith, family, and where you come from shape what you carry forward. That matters as much as what you believe now. Chapter Three: This moment needs something different. You do not step forward because you want the title. You step forward because the moment demands change. Growing means being willing to choose what is right over what is expected. Change is not weakness. It is strength.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: David Jolly is a former Member of Congress, attorney, and nationally recognized television analyst who launched his bid for Governor in June of 2025. Since announcing his candidacy, David has traveled every corner of the state, hosting hundreds of town halls and community forums focused on improving the state’s economy. A person of deep faith, David believes everyone deserves a shot at work, wages, and wealth, and that their rights should be protected and their dignity celebrated, regardless of the color of one’s skin, where they were born, who they love, or who they worship.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: David has focused his campaign on historic groundbreaking homeowner’s insurance reform, the expansion of primary healthcare services, and investing in more community public schools. A fifth-generation Floridian and son of a minister, David and his wife Laura are raising their young family in Pinellas County.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: David’s political story is one of change. While in Congress, he was known as a common-sense Republican working across the aisle on issues like campaign finance reform, gun violence prevention, reproductive freedom, and the environment. His fight to take on Washington corruption was featured on CBS’ 60 Minutes. David then spent seven years as an independent, organizing voters throughout the country around democracy protection, ending gerrymandering, opening primaries, and reforming our broken campaign finance laws.

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: Today, David is a proud Florida Democrat, fighting for the values he sees rooted in democratic tradition, that the economy should work for everyone; responsible investments in housing, healthcare, and education can improve people’s lives; and, everyone’s rights should be protected regardless of their walk of life. David’s willingness to lead with conviction led the Tampa Bay Times to write, “It’s refreshing to hear someone take on the system.” One Washington Post columnist famously penned, “Jolly speaks the truth.” And upon leaving Congress, another columnist wrote, “Farewell to the one Congressman willing to compromise.”

chunks.title: Meet David Jolly — Florida Governor 2026
chunks.text: In addition to his work in Congress and in the private practice of law, David served for nearly a decade as a political analyst on NBC and MSNBC. His work has been featured in Time, USA Today, Roll Call, The Washington Post, The New York Times, CNN, NBC, and The Tampa Bay Times. David received a Bachelor’s degree from Emory University and a Juris Doctor Cum Laude from George Mason.
